source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/Page_2020_AHAStatement.pdf, online-first version, pp. e1-e22 (all pages read in a text extraction; Table 3 on pp. e11-e13 and pp. e9-e10, e13-e14 and e17 checked on rendered pages). The statement has no methods section: no search, selection or appraisal method is described, and Table 3 is titled as seminal studies.

claims.overstatement: None in the statement, which is cautious and matches the AHA's own judgment. The magnitude's Parekh entries 3.12 and 2.63 omit part of the exposure (see note).
claims.note: Supported by Page: the writing group's judgment that the evidence is still inconclusive (e10); 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use among 3,882 patients, printed without an interval (Table 3, e12), and the 9 patients who had used within the hour (e17); Hemachandra 3.3 (1.8-6.3), 2.3 (1.1-4.5) after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco, 4.7 (2.1-10.7) with weekly or more frequent use and no elevation with less frequent use (e12); Parekh 1.82 (1.08-3.10), and 2.45 (1.31-4.60) with use on more than 10 days a month, adjustment set not stated (e14; ref 68 is Stroke 2020, so the claim can give the year); Chami & Kim 1.37% vs 0.54%, RR 2.53 (2.45-2.61), adjustment not stated (e11); the selection-bias warning (e10), whose reference list for hospital-based signals includes Chami & Kim; CARDIA (Reis et al. 2017; e12); Frost 29% higher, 95% CI 0.81-2.05, P=0.28 (e11; 'long-term' comes from the reference title); Desai 2019, 0.23% vs 0.14% (e11); Johnson-Sasso OR 0.79 (e12); the listed weaknesses (e9); evidence insufficient especially for people with cardiac risk factors (e17); one cannabis cigarette shortened exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo in people with chronic stable angina (e17; ref 88, a 1974 study). Editors' conversion checked: 1.37% and 0.54% are 13.7 and 5.4 per 1,000 (about 14 and 5); 1.37/0.54 = 2.54, matching RR 2.53. Not supported as worded: (1) Parekh 3.12 (1.40-6.97) and 2.63 (1.07-6.46) are for frequent cannabis use together with combustible-cigarette use or with e-cigarette use, against people who did not use cannabis (e17); the magnitude gives them as use with combustible cigarettes and with e-cigarettes, without 'frequent' or the comparison group (Page does not restate the threshold there; its earlier sentence defines frequent use as more than 10 days a month). (2) The magnitude labels Hemachandra's 3.3 'unadjusted'; Page gives it only as the estimate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates, without saying whether it was crude. (3) 'In-hospital' for Johnson-Sasso's OR 0.79 is not stated in Page (the reference title says short-term outcomes in patients hospitalised for myocardial infarction), and no interval or adjustment is printed. Missing for balance: Page reports (e17; Table 3, e11) that cannabis use, present in 6% of patients aged 50 or younger with a heart attack, is associated with worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality (DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults: adjusted HR 1.99 and 2.22, given in the table for cocaine and marijuana use together); the claim's evidence after a heart attack lists only a non-significant estimate (Frost) and a lower one (Johnson-Sasso). Page also qualifies the mortality gradient relayed from Hall & Degenhardt (2.5 and 4.2 times): smaller studies (refs 37 and 87, Frost 2013 and Mukamal 2008) showed a signal toward higher mortality, but many findings were not statistically significant (e17). And Table 3 lists a 2019 systematic review (Richards et al.) in which 28 of 33 studies suggested a higher risk of acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease (e12).

anchors.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 7th paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Overall the evidence is still inconclusive for cannabis use and adverse cardiovascular outcomes; carefully designed prospective short- and long-term studies are urgently needed.

anchors.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 2nd paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Most available data are short term, observational and retrospective; exposure not determined; recall bias; minimal exposure with no dose or product standardisation; usually low-risk cohorts; many studies may be confounded by access to health care and other behaviours such as tobacco use; rising THC concentrations may make earlier studies less relevant.

anchors.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 3rd paragraph (begins e9 right column)
anchors.extracted: Few data from rigorous prospective cohorts. CARDIA (adults aged 18-30 followed for more than 25 years; 84% with a history of use): cumulative lifetime and recent use not associated with incident cardiovascular disease, coronary heart disease or cardiac mortality. Several studies show signals of adverse cardiac outcomes, mostly in hospitalised patients with inherent selection bias (refs 28, 31-36, 40, 41, 43, 45, 49); when hospitalised patients with cannabis use are cases and those without are controls, a high probability of selection bias exists.

CARDIA, baseline 1985-1986, 5,113 adults aged 18-30, followed for more than 25 years; 84% reported use; cumulative lifetime and recent use not associated with incident cardiovascular disease, stroke or TIA, coronary heart disease or cardiac mortality; no estimates printed. (Evidence against harm, reported as such in the claim.)

Explorys aggregate database 2011-2016: 292,770 patients with a history of cannabis use (called the cannabis abuse group in the results column; reference title: cannabis abuse and myocardial infarction in the young) and more than 10 million controls; 3-year cumulative incidence of acute myocardial infarction 1.37% vs 0.54%; RR 2.53 (95% CI 2.45-2.61); adjustment not stated.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Desai et al. (2019, ref 33) row
anchors.extracted: National Inpatient Sample 2007-2014, more than 52 million hospitalisations, cannabis use without other substance use: admissions of young adults for acute myocardial infarction 0.23% with cannabis use vs 0.14% without; arrhythmia and stroke more frequent, venous thromboembolism less frequent.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Hemachandra et al. row; text on p. e10, Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: PATH Through Life population survey (1999-2002; ages 20-24 n=2,383, 40-44 n=2,525, 60-64 n=2,547): people with past-year use (n=1,043) had 3.3 times the rate of stroke or TIA (95% CI 1.8-6.3; P<0.001); after adjustment for stroke-related covariates including tobacco smoking, IRR 2.3 (1.1-4.5); elevated with weekly or more frequent use (IRR 4.7, 2.1-10.7), no elevation with less frequent use. The text gives the age-group sizes as 2,404, 2,530 and 2,551.

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Young Adults, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Parekh et al. (ref 68, Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System): higher odds of stroke with cannabis use at ages 18-44, adjusted OR 1.82 (95% CI 1.08-3.10) against people who did not use cannabis; with frequent use (more than 10 days a month) adjusted OR 2.45 (1.31-4.60). Adjustment set not stated.

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Patients With Cardiac Risk Factors, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: At ages 18-44, against people who did not use cannabis, stroke risk higher among people with frequent cannabis use and concomitant combustible-cigarette use (adjusted OR 3.12, 95% CI 1.40-6.97) and e-cigarette use (2.63, 1.07-6.46) (ref 68). Limited longitudinal data and recall bias in cross-sectional studies; the present evidence for a link between health outcomes and cannabis use, especially in patients with cardiac risk factors, is insufficient.

anchors.locator: Table 3, Mittleman et al. row; text on p. e17, Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Case-crossover study, 3,882 patients with acute myocardial infarction: risk of onset 4.8 times baseline in the 60 minutes after use (no interval); people who used were more often men, cigarette smokers and obese. Text: 3% had smoked cannabis in the prior year; 37 within 24 hours and 9 within 1 hour of presentation.

Determinants of MI Onset Study with National Death Index, 3,886 patients with myocardial infarction: mortality rate 29% higher with cannabis use than without, not significant (95% CI 0.81-2.05; P=0.28); adjustment not stated. Reference title: long-term mortality among survivors.

Hospital records from 8 states (1994-2013), more than 1.2 million patients with acute myocardial infarction, 3,854 (about 0.3%) reporting cannabis use: composite of death, balloon pump, mechanical ventilation, cardiac arrest or shock not associated with use; lower mortality with use (OR 0.79; no interval or adjustment printed). Reference title: short-term outcomes in patients hospitalised for myocardial infarction.

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, 1st paragraph (left column; continues in right column)
anchors.extracted: Cannabis raises myocardial oxygen demand and lowers supply, so people with ischaemic disease could have more angina, particularly when cannabis is smoked. In chronic stable angina, one cannabis cigarette decreased exercise time to angina by 48% against placebo (ref 88, 1974). In coronary disease with angina, use was associated with lower end-diastolic volume, stroke index and ejection fraction (ref 89).

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Comorbid Cardiovascular Disease, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cannabis use present in 6% of patients aged 50 or younger with acute myocardial infarction and associated with worse all-cause and cardiovascular mortality (ref 32; Table 3, p. e11: DeFilippis et al. 2018, 2,097 young adults with myocardial infarction, adjusted HR 1.99 all-cause and 2.22 cardiovascular mortality for cocaine and marijuana use together). Smaller studies show a signal toward higher mortality in coronary disease with cannabis use, although many findings were not statistically significant (refs 37, 87).

anchors.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 1st paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: THC stimulates the sympathetic and inhibits the parasympathetic nervous system, raising heart rate, myocardial oxygen demand, supine blood pressure and platelet activation (no dose relation or tolerance stated here); CBD may lower heart rate and blood pressure.

Systematic review of 85 studies, case reports and case series (541,581 adults): of 33 studies evaluated, 28 suggested a higher risk of acute coronary syndrome and chronic cardiovascular disease with cannabis use; in 51 case reports or series (62 people), 14 deaths (23%) attributed to acute coronary syndrome.

anchors.locator: Safety Considerations › Cardiac- and Vascular-Specific Effects, 4th paragraph (left column); Table 3, Auer et al. row, p. e11
anchors.extracted: Among people who had ever smoked tobacco, cannabis use was associated with more abdominal and coronary artery calcification; among people who never smoked tobacco, no association (CARDIA, 3,498; the text cites ref 46 for this, Table 3 ref 29).

claims.note: Page relays Crume et al. (ref 70, J Pediatr 2018) with the adjustment set the claim gives; the claim can add the year. Exposure is self-reported prenatal use at any time in pregnancy (prevalence 5.7%). Page also relays Gunn et al. (ref 71) with the claim's figures (anaemia 1.36, low birth weight 1.77, mean difference 109.42 g printed as a positive number) in causal-leaning wording (the meta-analysis is said to have demonstrated these, and the odds ratio is called a higher risk), which the claim rightly does not adopt.

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: In a state with legalised medical and recreational cannabis (Crume et al., ref 70): self-reported cannabis use at any time in pregnancy 5.7% (plus or minus 0.5); prenatal use associated with a 50% higher likelihood of low birth weight independently of maternal age, race or ethnicity, education and tobacco use in pregnancy (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1-2.1; P=0.02).

anchors.locator: Considerations in Special Populations › Pregnant Women, 1st paragraph (right column)
anchors.extracted: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Gunn et al., ref 71): maternal anaemia OR 1.36 (1.10-1.69); low birth weight OR 1.77 (1.04-3.01); pooled mean difference in birth weight 109.42 g (38.72-180.12), printed as positive.

key_findings.note: Counts checked on the rendered Table 3: 25 rows (refs 19, 26-49), 7 National Inpatient Sample rows, intervals in 5 rows, no figures in the Auer, Bancks and Lorenz rows.
The citation swap and the missing stroke or TIA in the text were found independently in the blind reading.
Small wording point in the note: the statement says 9 had smoked within 1 hour of AMI presentation (p. e17), not of onset; the timing used in the primary should be taken from Mittleman et al. (2001).

key_findings.correction: The statement says that many of the findings of the smaller mortality studies failed to reach statistical significance (p. e17), not that they mostly did; replace 'mostly not significant' with 'many not significant'. The rest is confirmed.

key_findings.note: Checked: five inpatient rows include 2010-2014 (refs 33-36, 45) and four share the first author Desai (refs 33-36).

The card keeps 'frequent use' for the Parekh co-use estimates (3.12, 2.63), which the claim cl_can_heart_vascular drops. The statement does not call Hemachandra's 3.3 unadjusted: it is the estimate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates (same point applies to the analysis field and RI 2).
The note's figures from card sc_monte_2019 cannot be checked from this source.
Ref 24 is Kaya et al. 2016, carboxyhaemoglobin and later myocardial infarction in carbon monoxide poisoning, as the card says.

key_findings.correction: The statement does not name Colorado: it describes Crume et al. as a study in a state with legalised medical and recreational cannabis (p. e14), and the title of ref 70 names no state. Drop 'in Colorado' or source it from the primary paper. The rest is confirmed (5.7% plus or minus 0.5; 5.0%, 4.1-6.2; OR 1.5, 1.1-2.1, P=0.02; the adjustment set; Gunn et al.'s figures with the mean difference printed without a sign).

key_findings.note: Flag under the no-advice rule: the sleep row's contrast between low and high doses is relayed as a finding without doses; any claim built on it must not read as advice on how much to use.
Checked on the rendered p. e3: the 43.5 million label is printed; the axis is in percent, but the measure and base are not stated; there is no age breakdown.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in the blind reading (refs 29 and 46 checked in the reference list).
One qualification: neither the text nor Table 3 calls the 3.3 unadjusted; it is the estimate before adjustment for stroke-related covariates.
Recomputed geometric midpoints: 6.95 for 3.0-16.1 and 3.00 for 2.2-4.1.
Checked: the sentence with 9%, 17% and 25-50% carries no citation (the sentence before cites refs 57, 58).
Figure 1 (rendered p. e2) defines hemp as cannabis with less than 0.3 THC (no unit printed).
The statement's own wording is as described; the comparison with the primary rests on card sc_monte_2019 and was not checked here.

risk_of_bias.note: Checked: no funding statement is printed; Rana is a co-author of refs 29, 30 and 46; Kloner of ref 22. Overall high follows the worst domains (search, appraisal, grading).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the body's own conclusions (inconclusive; insufficient for people with cardiac risk factors) match the evidence. It is the upper edge of minor: the abstract's framing and the sentence attributing worse mortality to cannabis from a combined cocaine-and-marijuana estimate go beyond the statement's own table.

missed: Hyperemesis (p. e13, Chronic Side Effects, uncited sentence): long-term heavy, THC-predominant use is associated with a higher risk of hyperemesis syndrome, with prodromal abdominal discomfort and nausea leading to intractable vomiting. The card has only the Table 2 row (KF 28).

Withdrawal advice (p. e18, Patient Education and Considerations): clinicians are told to advise people who use long term and heavily not to stop suddenly, because of the risk of withdrawal syndrome, and to seek care if withdrawal or hyperemesis symptoms arise. No evidence is cited. It sits uneasily with the statement in cl_can_withdrawal (from Connor et al., 2021) that withdrawal carries no serious risk; if used, report it as the AHA's recommendation, not as evidence.

Withdrawal time course (p. e13; KF 25 has it): onset a few days after stopping, peak at about 10 days, end after about 30 days (refs 5, 12). This differs from the time course in cl_can_withdrawal (peak within the first week, fading within 1-2 weeks), which does not cite this statement; the editor may want to note the disagreement.
